name: Bianca Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work Highmoor Farm with my uncle Peter. It's been in our family four generations. We've got 150 suckler cows, so beef cows that raise their own calves, plus hay and some barley on 300 hectares of hill ground. I'm up at six, feed round in winter, checking cows and fences the rest of the year, and lambing for a neighbour in spring because she's short-handed.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love that it's ours. My grandfather built the stone barn with his brother. What wears me out is the hill in February, when everything's frozen and you're carrying water. I don't use any of the AI things, I've got no need. Peter's hopeless with computers too, so it's paper and a calendar on the kitchen wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now people can get back to real work. I'd say that at church coffee after the service and probably at the market. I don't do online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a relief. The farm carries on the way it's always been, and that's what I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing. Same cows, same hill. Keep saving like I always have. The wedding's next summer and that's paid for already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you have no need for AI. Has anyone tried to change your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The feed rep, every visit. He shows me an app on his tablet. I tell him the cows don't read.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's on your mind for the year ahead in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wedding, honestly. Mark and I are getting married at St Anne's in the village in July. And whether Peter's ready to hand over more of the decisions to me. That's the real change I'm waiting for.

S0.say: Good, now people can get back to real work. I'd say that at church coffee after the service and probably at the market.
S0.think: It's a relief, because the farm carries on the way it's always been. That's what I want for Highmoor and for us.
S0.do: Changes nothing on the farm and keeps saving as always. Goes ahead with a wedding next summer that's already paid for.
S0.quote: He shows me an app on his tablet. I tell him the cows don't read.
S0.fieldNote: Bianca's life is rooted in family land, church and a wedding next July. The plateau confirms what she hopes for. The real change on her mind is her uncle handing over control, not technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine for the big farms down in the valley, but it's not for hill farms. You can't put a robot on a slope like ours. I'd say that at the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm not sure that's true. Peter's getting older and his knees are bad. If a machine could do the feed round, he'd want it, and I'd have to learn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing in the first year. I'd see what the neighbours do. If it really worked on hill ground, I'd think about it, but not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Like a cow you know is going to calve wrong but hasn't started yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Peter buy anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. He listens to the young rep more than to me sometimes, which annoys me. If the rep showed him a feeder that saves his knees, he'd sign up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mark about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd keep the cows and he'd keep the machines working. He's an electrician, he'd love it. We'd probably argue about it at dinner.

S1.say: It's fine for the big valley farms but not for hill farms, because you can't put a robot on a slope like ours.
S1.think: I'm not sure that's true. Peter's knees are bad, and if a machine could do the feed round he'd want it, and I'd have to learn it.
S1.do: Does nothing in the first year and watches what neighbours do. Would consider a machine only if it clearly worked on hill ground.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy, like waiting for a difficult calving.
S1.quote: If the rep showed him a feeder that saves his knees, he'd sign up.
S1.fieldNote: Her public line about hill farms being safe isn't what she privately believes. The threat comes from her uncle's age and health, not from losing her job. She and her fiancé would split the work between cows and machines, though not without arguing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to stand on their own feet and look after their families and communities, because the government won't. I'd say we should be careful what we hand over to machines. That's what I'd say at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it frightens me. If robots can do everything on a farm, what's Highmoor for? Four generations of my family working that hill, and I'd be the one who just watches it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep farming, with my own hands, for as long as anyone buys the beef. I'd put more by, and I'd lean on the family and the church. I wouldn't buy a robot. If prices fell so far that we couldn't sell, then we'd have to think again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Not about money so much. About what the point of it all is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'll own the land one day. Doesn't that protect you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It protects the money, yes. Grandad left me 20 hectares of my own and we'll get Highmoor in time. But land with nobody working it isn't a farm. It's a view.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. Would the wedding still go ahead as planned?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. If anything I'd want it sooner. When things are falling apart, you hold on to the people you've got.

S2.say: People need to stand on their own feet and look after their families and communities, because the government won't. We should be careful what we hand over to machines.
S2.think: It frightens me, because if robots can do everything on a farm, what's Highmoor for? Four generations worked that hill, and I'd be the one who just watches it.
S2.do: Keeps farming by hand for as long as the beef sells, refuses to buy a robot and saves more. Leans on family and church and wants the wedding brought forward.
S2.feel: Scared, mainly about losing the point of her life's work rather than money.
S2.quote: But land with nobody working it isn't a farm. It's a view.
S2.fieldNote: Money isn't the threat for her, since she owns land outright. The threat is to identity and family meaning, which hits harder for someone who never uses AI and dislikes change. Her instinct in a crisis is to hold on to people: family, church, an earlier wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and villages should get ready together. Teach the young ones a trade, keep the land in local hands. I wouldn't be asking for handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for Peter to retire and hand me the farm. Then it's my choice what we do. That's a lot to carry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working the herd. I'd talk to Peter about the handover, so the farm's legally mine and Mark's before things change. I'd vote for whoever promised to protect family farms from big companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's a slower version of the same fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, would you change your mind about not buying a robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe one machine, for Peter's knees. Not for the cows. The cows I'd keep doing myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you hold responsible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big companies, mostly, and the people in cities who think food comes from a shop. Not the government, because I don't expect much from them anyway.

S3.say: Families and villages should get ready together, teaching the young ones a trade and keeping the land in local hands. I wouldn't be asking for handouts.
S3.think: Five years is enough for Peter to retire and hand me the farm, and then it's my choice what we do. That's a lot to carry.
S3.do: Keeps working the herd and pushes her uncle to complete the legal handover of the farm to her and her husband. Votes for whoever promises to protect family farms from big companies.
S3.feel: Anxious, a slower version of the same fear.
S3.quote: Maybe one machine, for Peter's knees. Not for the cows.
S3.fieldNote: The five-year version shifts her attention to the legal handover of the farm. She blames big companies and city people, not government, because she expects little from government. She'd make one practical exception to her refusal, out of care for her uncle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's plenty of time, so families should plan sensibly. Keep the young ones grounded and the land in the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels further off. I'd half believe it. Peter would say they promised flying cars too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Have the wedding, start a family, take over from Peter bit by bit. I'd wait and see if it's really coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but there's a lot else going on in ten years. Babies, I hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. By then you'd be 37, maybe with children. How does that change it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot. I'd want my children to grow up on the farm like I did. I'd want them to know how to pull a calf, even if a robot could do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think you'd still be farming by hand in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of it. Maybe less. I'd be a mother by then and I can't be in two places. But I'd keep the cows. That's not changing.

S4.say: There's plenty of time, so families should plan sensibly. Keep the young ones grounded and the land in the family.
S4.think: Ten years feels further off and I'd only half believe it. Peter would say they promised flying cars too.
S4.do: Carries on with the wedding, starting a family and taking over from her uncle bit by bit. Waits to see whether AGI is really coming before changing anything.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but with plenty of other life going on.
S4.quote: I'd want them to know how to pull a calf, even if a robot could do it.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, her family plans take centre stage and the worry fades into the background. She wants to pass on hands-on skills to future children whatever the machines can do. She admits she'd work by hand less once she has children.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one. There'd be no time to hand the farm over properly or to work out what Highmoor is for. What would help is rules that keep land with families who work it, so the big companies can't buy up the hills for their robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about church. Half the village is there on a Sunday. If people lose their work, that's where they'd come. I'd want it to still be there.

headlineQuote: When things are falling apart, you hold on to the people you've got.
portrait: Bianca Hansen is a 27-year-old hill farmer working her family's 300-hectare beef farm alongside her uncle, and she'll inherit it in time. She never uses AI, keeps the farm on paper, goes to church and is marrying an electrician next summer. She's calm in the mild pictures and frightened by AGI in two years, not for money, since she owns land, but because she can't see what the farm would be for. With more time she focuses on the legal handover, her family and passing on hands-on skills, and she blames big companies and city people rather than government.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there'd be no time to hand the farm over properly or work out what it is for.
whatWouldHelp: Rules that keep land with the families who work it, so big companies can't buy up the hills for robots.
